name: Treadmill desk
lead: A treadmill desk is a computer desk adapted so the user walks slowly on a treadmill while working. It is intended to reduce sitting time and raise energy expenditure above resting levels, not to deliver aerobic exercise.[1]

Wikipedia credits Nathan Edelson with proposing the idea in the late 1980s, and James Levine of the Mayo Clinic is credited as its popular inspiration.[1] Trials and reviews report increased activity and energy expenditure and modest weight changes, with limited evidence of cardiometabolic benefit.[1][2][3]

paras: Edelson published articles in 1988 and 1989 and received a patent in 1993 for a portable version. Seth Roberts built one in 1996, and Levine popularised the concept. TrekDesk, the first height-adjustable desk made to fit existing treadmills, appeared in 2009.[1]

Three categories exist: desks fitted over a standard treadmill, treadmills fitted under standing desks, and integrated units. Safety features include a clip-on key that stops the belt and automatic pausing when no user is present.[1]

A 1-year prospective trial of 36 employees tested whether treadmill desks would raise daily activity and cut sedentary time.[4] Levine's team reported mean weight loss of 1.4 kg, or 2.3 kg among obese participants, per Wikipedia.[1] A 2021 meta-analysis of 13 studies, as summarised on Wikipedia, found increased energy expenditure and modestly less sitting but lacking evidence of cardiometabolic benefit.[1] Systematic reviews of standing and treadmill desks and of active workstations have assessed health and performance outcomes.[2][3] A randomized controlled trial evaluated a workplace treadmill desk intervention, and a study examined physicians' activity.[7][8] Acute cardiometabolic markers were assessed after reducing prolonged sitting with a treadmill desk.[9]

Studies tested cognitive tasks while walking slowly. One examined Stroop, flanker and reading comprehension in 66 participants.[10] Another study reported that slow walking did not negatively affect executive abilities.[11] A PLOS ONE study of 75 participants reported a modest negative effect on number-sequence recall, and Levine reported lower mouse accuracy, per Wikipedia.[1] A study examined transcriptionists' productivity.[12]

timeline.event: Edelson granted patent for a portable version.[1]

card.summary: Walk-while-you-work setup; trials show more movement and small weight changes, not posture or looks.
card.note: Evidence for cardiometabolic benefit is limited; may affect fine motor tasks.

quick.overview:
A treadmill desk lets you walk slowly, usually under 2 mph, while working at a computer. It is designed to break up sitting time rather than provide a workout.

Trials report more daily activity and modest weight changes; cardiometabolic benefits are not established.[1]
quick.mechanism: Slow walking raises energy expenditure above resting levels while the user types or reads.[1]
quick.risks: Studies report slight effects on pointing accuracy and number recall. Safety keys stop the belt if the user steps off.[1]
